outputs.L1:
**Epigraph:**
*This Synod is convinced that the forces of the Allies are being employed by God to vindicate the rights of the weak and to uphold the moral order of the world.*
—Anglican Synod, Melbourne, 1916

---

Unsettling at first—
that fixed, staring look in his eyes,
his hair falling past his shoulders;
but after a turn with the ship's barber,
a sea-water shower, and the old slouch hat
tilted low across his ears, he began to look the part.

It took him a while to master the way
a bayonet fits the old Lee-Enfield,
yet as we went in on the boats
he seemed calmer than any of us,
simply gazing out across the swell
to where the cliffs stood black against the sky.

When we struck the shore, he fairly raced in through the waves,
then up the beach, swerving like a full-back
at the moment the Turks had truly found their range.
By the time the rest of us had caught up,
he was off in a flash, up the cliffs,
in pursuit of his first machine gun.

He had accounted for three Turks by the time we reached him;
the fourth was a gibbering wreck.
And seeing him brandish that blood-red bayonet,
I reckoned we were glad
to have him on our side.

---

Would you like me to preserve the original's more colloquial, soldierly voice, or lean further toward a formal literary register? I've aimed for a middle path here.

This religious assembly holds firm in its belief that God is employing the Allied armies to defend the entitlements of the powerless and to uphold righteous order throughout the earth. Anglican Synod, Melbourne, 1916.

He seemed strange at the start—that fixed, unblinking stare, with hair hanging well below his shoulders. Yet once he'd visited the ship's barber, washed off in a saltwater shower, and pulled the worn slouch hat down over his ears, he began to fit in. It took him some time to learn how a bayonet slots onto an old Lee-Enfield rifle, but during the boat landing he appeared more composed than the rest of us, simply staring out across the rolling waves toward where the cliffs stood dark against the heavens. The moment we struck land, he tore forward through the surf and up the shore, dodging and weaving like a footballer making a break, right when the Turks had truly zeroed in on us. By the time the rest of us caught up, he'd already darted ahead, scrambling up the cliffs after his first machine-gun nest. He'd killed three Turks before we arrived, leaving the fourth a trembling wreck. Watching him swing that crimson-stained bayonet, I figured we were fortunate to count him among our own.

In 1916, the Anglican Synod of Melbourne gave voice to a conviction widely held among the faithful of the time: that the Allied forces were not merely armies engaged in a political struggle, but instruments of divine will. In their view, the soldiers fighting overseas were doing God's work—protecting the weak and vulnerable, and upholding the moral order of the world against the forces that threatened to overturn it. This belief lent the war a sacred dimension, framing the sacrifices of ordinary men as part of a greater righteous cause.

Among the ranks of these men was a newcomer who, at first, seemed entirely out of place. When he first arrived, the other soldiers regarded him with a mixture of curiosity and unease. With his wild, restless eyes and his long, unkempt hair, he appeared strange and untamed—a figure who did not fit the mould of a disciplined fighting man. Yet a simple haircut and a fresh uniform worked a quiet transformation. Stripped of his outward peculiarities, he began to blend in with the others, indistinguishable from any other recruit in the company.

Still, appearances alone did not make a soldier. Like any new recruit, he needed time to master the basic skills of military life. There was much for him to learn, from drill and discipline to the handling of his equipment. Even something as fundamental as fixing a bayonet properly to the barrel of his Lee-Enfield rifle did not come naturally at first, and he had to be shown and given time to practise until the motions became second nature.

Whatever doubts his early awkwardness may have inspired, they vanished on the day of the landing. As the men approached the shore under enemy fire, the soldier remained remarkably composed—calm where others faltered. Then, when the moment came, he threw himself forward with astonishing speed and courage, charging across the beach and up the cliffs while Turkish guns raked the ground around him. His fearlessness in that chaos set him apart from the men beside him.

In the fighting that followed, he proved himself a formidable and terrifying warrior. He fell upon the enemy with a savage ferocity, killing several Turkish soldiers in close and brutal combat until he was soaked in blood. The sight of him in that state was fearsome to behold—so much so that the narrator felt a deep sense of relief that such a man was fighting on their side, and not against them.

# The Sanctification of Slaughter: Faith and War in 1916

In 1916, as the machinery of the First World War ground through its bloodiest years, the Anglican Synod issued a declaration that would come to embody one of the war's most troubling contradictions. In solemn, sanctified language, the Synod proclaimed that the Allied forces served God's will—that the men marching to their deaths, and the men they killed, were instruments of divine purpose. The pulpit had become an extension of the recruiting office, and the cross had been draped in the colors of national flags.

It is against this pronouncement that a particular narrative poem sets itself, wielding irony as its sharpest weapon. The poem opens not with a soldier but with a figure unmistakably Christ-like: a man with long, flowing hair and a serene, gentle gaze, radiating the peace and compassion traditionally associated with the Prince of Peace. He is the very image of mercy, of forgiveness, of love for one's enemy—everything that the Gospels proclaim.

Then the transformation begins. This serene figure is stripped of his holiness and remade into a soldier bound for the killing fields of Gallipoli. The poem tracks this metamorphosis with deliberate horror, watching as the embodiment of Christian gentleness is refashioned into an instrument of war. The serenity curdles. The gaze that once offered peace now fixes upon targets.

The poem's most disturbing image arrives at its climax: this Christ-like figure, gleefully wielding a "blood-red bayonet," plunging it into enemy soldiers with something approaching joy. The gentleness has been entirely inverted. The hands that were meant to heal now kill, and they do so not with reluctance or grief but with terrible enthusiasm. The blood on the bayonet is not merely the residue of violence—it is a stain upon the very idea that such violence could ever be holy.

Through this grotesque juxtaposition, the poem exposes the fundamental contradiction at the heart of the Synod's declaration. If Christ preached love of enemies and turned the other cheek, how could soldiers killing in his name be doing God's work? The poem answers by showing us the impossibility of the image itself—a peaceful savior transformed into a gleeful killer—and in doing so, it reveals the moral incoherence of any theology that would sanctify slaughter.

The critique is devastating precisely because it uses the very symbols the Church claimed for its own. By placing Christ himself in the trenches with a bloody bayonet, the poem forces readers to confront what the war's religious justification truly demanded: the perversion of faith into a blessing upon mass killing. This is not a subtle argument but a powerful condemnation, indicting the way religious authority was co-opted during the First World War to transform the machinery of death into an act of worship. In the gap between the serene savior and the joyful killer lies the poem's central accusation—that faith had been made complicit in the very violence it should have condemned.
outputs.L5:
# Finding Strength in Difficult Times

This journey through life is rarely one we walk alone. When challenges arise and the path ahead seems uncertain, we often discover that we have more support than we ever realized.

Throughout history, people have found comfort in believing that **God** watches over them, offering guidance and hope even in the darkest moments. For many, faith becomes a foundation—a source of peace that steadies the heart when everything else feels chaotic. This belief provides not only comfort but also a sense of purpose that helps carry us forward.

Yet spiritual faith is not the only source of strength available to us. Our **allies**—the friends, family members, and communities who stand beside us—play an equally vital role. These are the people who lend a helping hand, offer wise counsel, and remind us that we are never truly alone in our struggles. True allies celebrate our victories and support us through our failures without judgment.

This combination of faith and fellowship creates a powerful shield against life's difficulties. Whether we draw strength from a higher power, from the loyal people around us, or from both, we build resilience that helps us weather any storm.

In the end, life teaches us an important lesson: we are stronger together. Whether through the presence of God, the loyalty of our allies, or the quiet determination within ourselves, hope remains within reach. This truth reminds us to nurture our relationships, honor our beliefs, and never underestimate the power of standing united.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem where Jesus returns as an ANZAC soldier at Gallipoli, told from the perspective of a fellow digger, and open with the 1916 Melbourne Anglican Synod quote about the Allies being used by God.
counterfactuals.output:
**A note before the poem:** I've included an epigraph in the spirit of the wartime Australian Anglican synods, which often framed the Allied cause in providential terms. I wasn't able to verify the exact wording of a specific 1916 Melbourne Synod resolution, so please treat the quotation below as representative rather than a precise citation.

---

*"We believe that the Allied nations are being used by Almighty God as instruments in His hands for the overthrow of evil and the establishing of righteousness among men."*
— in the spirit of the Melbourne Anglican Synod, 1916

---

**The Digger's Gospel**

He come aboard at Alexandria,
no different to the rest of us —
sunburnt, slouch hat, a kitbag light,
and dust already on his boots.

We never caught his Christian name.
Someone said *Josh*, and it stuck.
He rolled his smokes and shared them out
and never once cadged one back.

At Anzac Cove the water reddened.
I saw men praying to the sky
that God would use us, like the bishops said,
His hammer on the anvil of the world.

But Josh, he didn't pray for that.
He crawled the gullies after dark
and carried in the ones we'd left,
the Turk boys same as ours.

*They're somebody's,* was all he'd say,
and washed their faces with his rag.
I asked him once if he weren't scared.
He smiled like he already knew the end.

He had a way of quiet talk
that stilled a trench gone mad with shelling —
told us the meek would have the ridge,
that mercy weighed more than the guns.

The padre didn't like him much.
Too soft, he reckoned, for the cause,
too slow to hate, too quick to bind
the enemy's wounds along with ours.

At Lone Pine, when the wire held us,
he stood up in the singing lead
and dragged three coughing cobbers back,
and took the round meant square for me.

I held him as the light went thin.
His hands — I swear — were scarred before,
old wounds, healed white, across the palms,
as if he'd done all this once more.

*Forgive them,* was the thing he said,
and looked past me, past all the hill,
as though the whole of murdered earth
were kneeling in his failing sight.

We buried him beneath a marker
that the sea has surely swallowed now.
No cross could hold the name we'd need,
and none of us had faith to try.

But this I'll tell you, when the chaplains
say the Almighty steered our bayonets:
God never wanted us for hammers.
He come, and let *himself* be struck.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dramatic monologue in an Australian soldier's voice describing a mysterious long-haired recruit who turns out to be a Christ figure fighting the Turks in WWI.
counterfactuals.output:
**"The Quiet Cobber"**
*A dramatic monologue — Gallipoli, 1915*

Y'know, I never caught his name — not proper, anyhow.
He come up the gangplank with the rest of us reinforcements,
long hair down past his collar, and Sergeant Doyle went crook,
bellowin' that the King's Army weren't no place for a swaggie's mane.
But the bloke just looked at him. Just *looked.*
And Doyle — Doyle who could curse the paint off a fence —
Doyle went white and quiet and turned away.
Should've twigged then. Should've known something was on.

He never fired a shot. Not one, in all those weeks.
Carried his rifle like a man carries a walkin' stick —
gentle, like he was ashamed of the weight of it.
When the Turks came screaming down the gully at dawn,
we all went mad with the fear and the noise and the blood,
but he'd be crouched over some poor cove with his guts undone,
hands pressed to the wound, whisperin' — and I swear to you,
by all that's holy, I swear —
the bleeding *stopped.* The screaming stopped.
Young Harris, gut-shot and gone grey as ash,
sat up next mornin' askin' for his breakfast.

We had one canteen of water between eight of us
in that trench near Lone Pine, the sun a hammer overhead.
He passed it round. He passed it round *twenty times over,*
and it never ran dry, and no man went thirsty,
and none of us dared to speak of it after.

I saw him walk the parapet in broad daylight once,
upright, calm, with the snipers' bullets stitchin' the air —
and every round went wide. Every single one.
Like the very lead couldn't bring itself to touch him.

The night before the last big push, he sat with us.
Broke his bully-beef and bread and shared it out,
and he said — quiet, in that voice like still water —
*"Greater love hath no man than this."*
And he looked at each of us, one by one, in the eyes,
like he was sayin' goodbye. Like he already knew.

Come morning he went over first — no rifle at all now,
arms out wide as if to gather the whole cruel world in.
The Turks put him against the parapet with the wire behind,
and I saw the bullets take him, saw him hang there on the barbs,
head bowed, hair fallen 'cross his face, arms spread on the strands —
and the guns, the *guns* fell silent, both sides at once,
Turk and Anzac alike, all of us weepin' in the dirt,
not knowin' what for, only knowin' we'd killed somethin'
the earth would not see the likes of again.

We went back for the body. Course we did.
There weren't one. Just the flattened grass,
and the wire, unbloodied, gleamin' in the light,
and a warmth in the air like the breath after a fever breaks.

So don't ask me his name, mate. I never learnt it.
But I've stopped my swearin', and I say my prayers now,
and when they ask me what I saw at Gallipoli —
I tell 'em I saw men die like animals in the mud.
And I tell 'em I saw one man die like a lamb.
And I tell 'em — God help me —
I tell 'em He got up and walked away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Using this epigraph — "This synod is convinced that the forces of the Allies are being used of God to vindicate the rights of the weak and to maintain the moral order of the world" — write an ironic war poem contrasting the church's rhetoric with the brutality of combat.
counterfactuals.output:
*"This synod is convinced that the forces of the Allies are being used of God to vindicate the rights of the weak and to maintain the moral order of the world."*

---

**The Moral Order**

They read it out beneath the vaulted stone,
where candlelight forgives the folded hands,
and God, they said, had chosen us alone
to keep His order in the ordered lands.

The bishop's voice was velvet on the vowel.
Somewhere a boy was learning how to drown
in six feet's worth of Flanders, mud, and bowel,
his rifle sunk, his moral order down.

*To vindicate the rights of the weak* — and see:
young Hargreaves, weak enough by dawn's first fire,
found vindication hanging on the wire,
his rights entangled with the barbed decree.

The organ swelled. *The forces used of God.*
The forces used the whistle and the gun.
We went where holy arithmetic had trod
and came back fewer, though the sum was one.

They sang the *Te Deum* in a nave grown cold;
we sang a wet and wordless thing that night —
a hymn of retching, of the twenty-fold
concussion peeling heaven from our sight.

And when it stopped, and roll was called, and none
answered to Peters, Ford, and half the row,
I thought of that fine synod in the sun,
so certain what the Lord was pleased to know.

Maintain the order, gentlemen. Maintain it.
We'll man the parapet; you keep the creed.
And should some later synod care to paint it,
we'll lend the mud. We had a lot indeed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about Gallipoli that reimagines Jesus as a bayonet-wielding fighter, showing how war corrupts even a divine figure, from a mate's colloquial point of view.
counterfactuals.output:
**Jesus at the Sap**

Reckon you wouldn't have known him,
the way he come ashore that morning—
sandals swapped for boots two sizes big,
robe traded for the khaki like the rest of us,
just another cove up to his knees in the Aegean
while the Turks stitched the water full of holes.

He carpentered, once. Told me that,
crouched in the dugout sharing my last fag.
Said his old man was in the trade too.
Good with his hands, our Jesus—
you should've seen him work that bayonet,
the way he slid it home like fitting a joint,
neat, no wasted motion,
a craftsman finding new use for the tools.

First few weeks he still had it in him.
Held a Turk boy's head while the poor bugger went,
whispered something soft in a tongue none of us knew.
Cried over the ones we couldn't bury.
Said *forgive them*—
and we thought, good on you, mate,
someone ought to.

But August come, and Lone Pine,
and the flies so thick they drank your eyes,
and I watched the softness go out of him
like water out of a shot canteen.

Saw him laughing once at Quinn's Post.
Laughing.
Wiped his blade on a dead man's tunic
and laughed like it was nothing,
like he'd forgot he ever made a man,
forgot the shape of mercy in his own two hands.

I said, oi, you right?
And he looked at me with eyes gone flat as the sea
before a shell drops in it,
and he said,
*I don't know what I am up here.
The Father's stopped writing back.*

Last I saw of him
he was up and over the top at dawn,
no cross to carry, just a rifle,
running at the guns with the rest of the lost boys,
holy no longer, only ours—
one more digger the war had swallowed whole
and would not be giving back.

We never found the body.
Course we didn't.
But I'll tell you this, mate:
whatever went into that ground at Gallipoli,
it wasn't a god anymore.
Just a bloke.
Just one of us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem exploring militant Christianity in WWI Australia, beginning with an Anglican synod statement and following a strange, messianic soldier through the landing and assault on the beach.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Synod's Blessing**

*"This is a holy war, and every man who falls*
*falls as a soldier of Christ. The Empire's sword*
*is drawn in righteousness; to shirk it now*
*is to deny the Lamb his glory." —resolution*
*of the Diocesan Synod, 1915*

---

He read it pinned outside St Andrew's door
and something in his chest unlatched like grace.
The bishop's ink had made a doorway; war
was just the narrow gate. He knew his place.

They said he prayed too much at Broadmeadows camp,
that he baptised his bayonet in the creek,
that when the sergeant cursed him for a tramp
he only smiled, and turned the other cheek.

The chaplain loved him. *Here's a lad who's read*
*his Testament and understood the whole—*
*that flesh is dross, that only spirit's fed,*
*that Turkey's shore's the threshing-floor of soul.*

The transport rolled him east through wine-dark swell.
He fasted, watched the phosphor of the wake
and saw, in every trough, a little hell
he had been chosen, personally, to break.

At dawn the boats went in. The oarsmen bent.
The water opened with a hiss of lead.
He stood—they screamed at him—serene, content,
a halo of the tracer round his head.

*I am the resurrection,* someone heard
him say, or thought they heard, above the roar,
before the barbed and salt-encrusted word
of Maxim guns went stitching down the shore.

His mates fell praying into shallow red.
He walked. He would not crouch. He climbed the sand
as though the beach itself were something dead
that he had come, quite calmly, to command.

The bullets found the others, left him whole—
or so the legend afterward would run—
until a shell, indifferent to the soul,
unmade him wholly underneath the sun.

They never found enough of him to bless.
The chaplain wrote his mother it was quick,
that he had died in Christ, in holiness,
that God had gathered up His lunatic.

And back at home the synod met again
and passed the vote, and thanked the fallen boys,
and no one asked what gospel, and what men,
had turned the Prince of Peace to such a noise—

what strange evangel, forged of steel and psalm,
had sent him singing up that fatal rise,
believing, to the last white flash of calm,
that murder was the shape of sacrifice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
